title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The future has TWO formations and which one a verb uses is decided by its family. habeō and labōrō take -bō: habēbō, labōrābō. legō, scrībō and veniō take -am in the first person and -ēs, -et after it: legam, legēs, leget. One tense, two patterns, and nothing in the meaning tells you which.

THE TRAP OF THIS MODULE: legēs is 'you WILL read' and docēs is 'you teach'. Same ending, different tense — because legō is a third-conjugation verb whose future borrows the -ēs, and doceō is a second-conjugation verb whose present already owns it. Only knowing the verb tells you which you are looking at.

The irregulars are irregular here too, and both are unavoidable: sum becomes erō ('I will be') and eō becomes ībō ('I will go'). Neither follows either pattern above, so they are learned as themselves — which is easier than it sounds, because you will use them constantly.

The present also does the future, exactly as in English. Crās eō is 'I am going tomorrow', and for a settled plan it is what a Roman would more often say. So there are three ways to talk about tomorrow: the real future, the present with crās, and volō plus an infinitive.
crās never changes shape and usually comes first, like herī and cotīdiē. Its ā is long — CRAS, held — and it is the only new word in this module that is not a verb.
A future is its own word, not a present with a helper in front. There is no 'will' and no 'shall' to put anywhere: the whole tense is inside the verb, which is the same lesson M5 taught about 'did'.

words.note: 'Tomorrow', and it never changes shape — an adverb like herī and cotīdiē. The ā is long: CRAS, held.
'I will come' — the future of M4's veniō, and it takes the -am pattern: veniam, veniet 'he will come'. There is no separate word for 'will'.

sentences.trap: Two words, and the second one contains the tense, the person and the verb. English needs three and one of them — 'will' — has no Latin counterpart at all.
sentences.sound: CRAS VE-ni-am. Hold the ā of crās. veniam is three light syllables with the stress at the front.

mistake.why: Two things: the English order for the wanting, which M3 and M4 both warned about, and the assumption that Latin needs a helper to point at the future. veniam is one word and says all of it.

words.note: 'Tomorrow', and it never changes shape — an adverb like herī and cotīdiē. The ā is long: CRAS, held.
'To, towards', and the noun after it takes the object shape — ad scholam, never ad schola.
'School' — schola as the subject, scholam after ad. In Latin it meant the teaching rather than the building.
'I will go' — the future of M4's eō, and irregular: ībō, ībit 'he will go'. Both vowels are long, which is most of what makes it recognisable.

sentences.trap: ībō is not eō with anything added. It is a different shape of the same tiny verb, and it has to be recognised rather than derived — which is true of both irregulars in this module.
sentences.sound: CRAS ad SCHO-lam I-bō. Two long vowels in ībō, said EE-boh, and the stress sits on the first.

mistake.why: The -bō ending bolted onto the present stem, which is how a regular first-conjugation verb would do it. eō is irregular and its future is ībō: there is no ending to attach because the stem itself changes.

sentences.mnemonic: eō goes, ībō will go. The vowel lengthens and moves.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. The e drops out as soon as an ending is added.
'I will read' — the future of M4's legō on the -am pattern: legam, legēs 'you will read', leget 'he will read'. Watch legēs; it is a future, not a present.

sentences.trap: legam looks like nothing in particular, and that is the difficulty: a third-conjugation future has no -b- in it, so there is no visible marker of futurity at all — only an ending you have to know.
sentences.sound: LI-brum LE-gam. Both stressed on the first syllable. Nothing here is long, which is itself a clue: the -bō futures all carry a long vowel and this pattern does not.

variations.changed: the second person — and the shape that collides with a present elsewhere
a third person on the same pattern

mistake.why: The -bō future built on a verb that does not take it. legō is third conjugation and its future is legam; habēbō is right for habeō and wrong here, and only the verb's family decides which.

words.note: 'Letter' — the written kind. epistula as the subject, epistulam as the object. English kept it in 'epistle'.
'I will write' — the future of M4's scrībō on the -am pattern: scrībam, scrībet 'he will write'. The ī stays long throughout the verb.

sentences.trap: scrībam and M5's scrīpsī are both 'the other' tense of scrībō, and neither is built from the present by adding anything. One changes the consonants and one changes the ending; the verb has to be learned in three pieces.
sentences.sound: e-PIS-tu-lam SCRI-bam. The long ī of scrībam is stressed; the -am is light.

mistake.why: A -bō future invented for a third-conjugation verb, and with an extra a for good measure. scrībam is the whole form; the pattern a verb uses cannot be guessed from its meaning or its shape.

sentences.usage: Said about correspondence you intend to write.
sentences.mnemonic: scrībō, scrīpsī, scrībam — present, past, future, three different words.

words.note: 'Tomorrow', and it never changes shape — an adverb like herī and cotīdiē. The ā is long: CRAS, held.
'Roman', bending for the person it describes: Rōmānus of a man, Rōmāna of a woman, Rōmānī of more than one. Both ō and ā are long.
'I will be' — the future of sum, and it shares nothing with either sum or M5's fuī: erō, erit 'he will be'. Three tenses, three unrelated stems.

sentences.trap: sum, fuī, erō. One verb, three shapes with almost no letters in common — and this is the verb you will need most often, so the irregularity is worth the effort rather than worth avoiding.
sentences.sound: CRAS ro-MA-nus E-rō. erō is E-roh with a long final vowel; it is short enough to be missed, so say it deliberately.

sentences.usage: Said about a change of state you expect.
sentences.mnemonic: sum, fuī, erō: am, was, will be, and no two alike.

words.note: 'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā as the thing needed. Three shapes of one word.
'I will have' — the future of M3's habeō, and this one DOES take -bō: habēbō, habēbit 'he will have'. Second-conjugation verbs all do.

sentences.trap: This is the pattern legam did not use. habeō is second conjugation and gets -bō; legō is third and gets -am. There is no way to tell from the English which family a verb is in.

'I will work' — the future of M4's labōrō, on the -bō pattern: labōrābō, labōrābit 'he will work'. Four syllables, three of them long.

sentences.trap: Four syllables for two English words. The a before the -bō is labōrō's own stem vowel, which M4 said it keeps — so the future is built on the shape you already know rather than on a new one.
sentences.sound: CRAS la-bō-RA-bō. Say it slowly: la-boh-RAH-boh. The stress sits on the third syllable because the ā there is long.

mistake.why: A plural ending on a sentence about one person. -bitis is 'you all will', and nothing in crās labōrābō suggests more than one worker — the person is chosen by the ending, so it has to be chosen deliberately.

sentences.mnemonic: labōrō keeps its a and takes the b: labōrābō.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. The e drops out as soon as an ending is added.
'You will read' — a FUTURE, though the -ēs ending is a present in second-conjugation verbs like doceō ('docēs', you teach). Only the verb's family tells them apart.

sentences.trap: legēs is a future and docēs is a present, and they look identical in their endings. There is no trick here: you have to know that legō is third conjugation and doceō is second, and the dictionary is where that lives.
sentences.sound: LI-brum le-GES. The stress moves onto the long ē, which it did not do in legam — the ending is carrying weight as well as meaning.

words.note: A Roman woman's given name, said YOO-li-a. Spelled with an i because Latin has no letter j at all.
'Tomorrow', and it never changes shape — an adverb like herī and cotīdiē. The ā is long: CRAS, held.
'I will come' — the future of M4's veniō, and it takes the -am pattern: veniam, veniet 'he/she will come'. There is no separate word for 'will'.

sentences.trap: Three tenses of this verb are now in play and all three third persons are short: venit, vēnit, veniet. The first is a bar away from the second and a syllable away from the third, and all three are in your vocabulary as of this module.
sentences.sound: YOO-li-a CRAS VE-ni-et. veniet is three syllables where venit is two — that extra syllable is the future, and it is easier to hear than the bar was.

variations.changed: the same words addressed TO her, so the verb becomes first person
the present doing the future's job — one syllable shorter
negated, with nōn against the verb

mistake.why: A bar taken from M5's past and put on a future. vēnit is 'she came' and veniet is 'she will come'; combining them produces a form that is neither, and the macron is the thing that makes the error visible at all.

sentences.mnemonic: venit, vēnit, veniet: comes, came, will come.

words.note: 'Tomorrow', and it never changes shape — an adverb like herī and cotīdiē. The ā is long: CRAS, held.
'She comes': veniō 'I come', venit 'he/she comes', venīre 'to come'. The -re ending is what makes it 'to', and the ī before it is long.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.trap: This is the third way to talk about tomorrow and the only one with no future tense in it. Latin can do the job with a tense, with a present, or with wanting — and a learner who only knows the tense will sound stiffer than a Roman.
sentences.sound: CRAS ve-NI-re VO-lō. The long ī of venīre takes the stress, which the short i of veniam did not.

mistake.why: A finite future where the infinitive belongs. volō governs an infinitive — venīre — and veniam is already a complete sentence, so this puts two verbs side by side with nothing joining them.
